Highlights
What are the main findings?
•
The event-based model combining a PointNet encoder with a bidirectional gated
recurrent unit network achieved a joint entry–exit count accuracy of 92.7% and a
mean absolute error of 0.06 persons per event in estimating occupancy change. When
applied without retraining or parameter adaptation in an independent laboratory, it
retained a joint count accuracy of 91.0%.
•
Geometric-consistency verification and the rejection of low-confidence decisions re-
duced cumulative counting errors, resulting in a mean absolute occupancy error of
0.10 person across five continuous sequences.
What are the implications of the main findings?
•
By treating a complete doorway passage as a single event, the proposed method uses
changes in point-cloud geometry, radial velocity, and their temporal evolution before,
during, and after temporary merging of reflections. It therefore does not require
continuous individual trajectories or frame-to-frame data association.
•
Bidirectional people counting can be performed using standard radar point clouds
generated by the device’s demonstration software, without using camera images as
model inputs, accessing raw analog-to-digital converter samples, or modifying the
radar firmware. The cross-environment experiment provides preliminary evidence of
transferability, although further validation across additional rooms, doorway widths,
participants, and radar mounting configurations is required.
Abstract
Accurate bidirectional people counting at room entrances is essential for reliable occupancy
estimation, yet radar-based methods remain challenged when reflections from multiple
individuals temporarily merge or when people move simultaneously in opposite directions.
This study presents a hybrid event-based method for bidirectional people counting using
a single 77 GHz multiple-input multiple-output frequency-modulated continuous-wave
radar. Unlike conventional tracking-based approaches, the proposed method treats a com-
plete doorway passage as one event and does not require continuous individual trajectories
or frame-to-frame data association. Each event is represented as a sequence of three-
dimensional point clouds with radial velocity information. A PointNet encoder extracts

frame-level spatial representations, a bidirectional gated recurrent unit models their tempo-
ral evolution, and an attention mechanism emphasizes the most informative event phases.
Separate output heads estimate the numbers of entering and exiting individuals, while an
auxiliary head identifies the event type. Predictions are accepted using explicit confidence
and geometric-consistency criteria. The primary dataset comprised 550 labeled events and
an additional 100 events recorded in five continuous sequences. In the held-out test session,
entry- and exit-count accuracies were 95.5% and 94.5%, respectively, while joint entry–exit
count accuracy reached 92.7%. The mean absolute error in occupancy change was 0.06
person per event, and the mean absolute occupancy error across the continuous sequences
was 0.10 person. The proposed method exceeded geometric rules and density-based clus-
tering combined with tracking in joint count accuracy by 37.2 and 24.5 percentage points,
respectively. On an independent laboratory dataset comprising 100 events, the model
achieved a joint count accuracy of 91.0% without retraining, fine-tuning, or parameter
adaptation, providing preliminary evidence of cross-environment generalization.
Keywords: mmWave radar; FMCW radar; MIMO radar; bidirectional people counting;
room occupancy estimation; radar point clouds; PointNet; BiGRU; attention mechanism
1. Introduction
Reliable information on the number of people occupying a room is an important
component of modern building management. It can be used to control ventilation, heating,
and air-conditioning systems, as well as to manage lighting, assess space utilization, and
support security systems [1]. Unlike simple presence detection, accurate people counting
enables the operation of building systems to be adjusted to the actual occupancy of a
room. This is particularly important in facilities where the number of occupants varies over
time and does not follow fixed operating schedules. Studies on occupancy-based control
of heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems confirm that information
on the actual presence and number of occupants can help reduce energy consumption
while maintaining the required indoor environmental quality [2]. In locations requiring
enhanced supervision, automated security systems can be developed using information
on the presence or density of people [3]. In commercial applications, information on the
number of customers near individual service points can be useful both for identifying
purchasing trends and for developing smart consumer services [4].
Occupancy monitoring technologies include passive infrared (PIR) sensors [5], optical
barriers [6], RGB cameras [7], thermal cameras [8], carbon dioxide concentration sensors [9],
and devices that monitor wireless network activity [10]. These solutions differ in the
scope of information they provide, their accuracy, and their impact on user privacy. PIR
sensors primarily detect movement and may fail to identify stationary occupants. CO2
concentration is an indirect indicator of occupancy, and its variation also depends on
ventilation performance, room volume, and previous usage patterns. Vision-based systems
provide rich spatial information; however, their effectiveness may be limited by changes in
illumination and occlusions between people, while image acquisition introduces additional
privacy-protection requirements.
Short-range radars operating in millimeter-wave frequency bands provide an alter-
native to optical sensors. Frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar enables
the contactless estimation of range and radial velocity and, in a multiple-input multiple-
output (MIMO) antenna configuration, the direction of arrival of the reflected signal [11].
Combining range, Doppler, and angular information provides a spatial representation of

the observed scene in the form of a radar point cloud. Radar operation does not require
illumination, and the acquired data do not contain direct images that would enable the
visual identification of individuals. These properties make radar systems suitable for use
in residential buildings, offices, and public facilities.
Previous applications of FMCW radar to people monitoring have included localization,
tracking, classification, and counting. Knudde et al. used a low-power 77 GHz MIMO
FMCW radar to track multiple people in an indoor environment [12]. The proposed pro-
cessing pipeline comprised beamforming, background modeling, false-detection removal,
and data association using Markov chain Monte Carlo data association (MCMCDA). The
feasibility of detecting, tracking, and classifying multiple people using a compact FMCW
radar was also demonstrated for a system operating at 24 GHz [13]. The robustness of
radar-based tracking was also investigated in scenarios involving multiple users located
near one another [14]. These studies did not directly count entries and exits but addressed
the detection and tracking stages subsequently employed in people-counting systems.
In conventional bidirectional people-counting systems, the direction of passage is typi-
cally determined from the trajectory relative to predefined lines or boundary regions. Yang
et al. developed a method using radar point clouds, multiscale clustering, and multi-object
tracking of extended targets [15]. Following range, angle, and velocity estimation, micro-
clustering, macroclustering, and refined clustering were applied sequentially, followed by
two-stage data association. The numbers of entering and exiting people were determined
from the resulting trajectories and the locations of the boundary regions.
A subsequent method accounted for interference caused by a moving door leaf [16].
Door-opening and door-closing events were detected using 4D radar data, after which
points associated with the door leaf were extracted and clustered. The door was then
incorporated into the tracking process as a separate target type. Different track-management
rules were applied to doors and people, whereas the numbers of entries and exits were
determined from the trajectories of the individuals and the locations of the boundary
regions. Owing to the design of both algorithms, counting accuracy depends on the quality
of point detection, clustering, data association, and the maintenance of valid trajectories for
the tracked individuals.
Counting people moving in proximity as a single group is particularly challenging. If
the distances between individuals are smaller than the radar’s range or azimuth resolution
and their velocities are similar, it becomes difficult to distinguish individual people based
on their positions and Doppler components. Ren et al. treated such a formation as a group
target and combined a multi-target tracking algorithm with a classifier that estimated
the number of people in each tracked group [17]. The classifier used features extracted
from range–azimuth maps and cadence–velocity diagrams (CVDs), and the method was
evaluated in outdoor scenarios. Wang et al. extended this approach to indoor environ-
ments by accounting for frequent changes in direction and stop-and-go motion [18]. They
employed extended Kalman filter-based tracking and a classifier using spatial features
extracted from range–azimuth maps and Doppler-frequency features obtained through
wavelet decomposition. The processing output was a time-varying estimate of the group’s
position and the number of people within it. Neither method requires a separate trajectory
to be extracted for each person in the group; however, both still combine an explicit group-
tracking module with a group-size classifier. Their outputs describe the current position
and size of the observed group rather than the numbers of entries and exits or cumulative
room occupancy.
In parallel, methods were developed in which the number of people was estimated
from sequences of radar signals without prior detection and tracking of individual tra-
jectories. Choi et al. developed Precent, whose input consisted of frames formed from

consecutive preprocessed one-dimensional range profiles [19]. Features from each profile
were extracted using a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN), tempo-
ral dependencies were modeled using a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM)
network, and the resulting representations were fused using an attention mechanism. The
feature extractor was pretrained in an unsupervised manner as part of a one-dimensional
convolutional autoencoder, after which the entire network was fine-tuned in a supervised
manner for people-count regression. The method demonstrated the feasibility of automat-
ically extracting features relevant to radar-based people counting. However, it used an
impulse-radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) radar rather than an FMCW radar, and the model
output represented the current number of people in the monitored area rather than an entry
or exit event or the cumulative room occupancy.
For FMCW radar, Aydogdu et al. used a 60 GHz radar and a two-channel repre-
sentation comprising two range–angle maps generated separately from the macro- and
micro-Doppler components [20]. The radar convolutional neural network was trained
both using radar data and through knowledge distillation from a vision-based network
processing synchronized camera images. During inference, only radar data were used.
The classifier distinguished classes corresponding to the presence of one, two, three, and
four people, as well as a class representing more than four people. The method estimated
the current number of people within the radar’s field of view but did not determine their
direction of movement. Cao et al. presented a solution more closely related to counting
people crossing an entrance [21]. The authors used range–time maps and a procedure
for extracting the portion of the map corresponding to a passage event based on Doppler
spectrum analysis. They subsequently applied a lightweight multiscale MFSNet within a
joint-learning architecture comprising multiple encoders and a classifier. Using a single
FMCW radar, the system simultaneously recognized the number of people passing through
the monitored area and their direction of movement.
Deep learning has also been applied to representations and features derived from
FMCW radar data acquired in the 24, 60, and 77 GHz frequency bands. Cakoni et al.
classified group size using micro-Doppler signatures obtained from a 77 GHz FMCW
radar [22]. The authors employed a custom CNN and compared its performance with
existing image-classification networks applied through transfer learning. Martín-Martín
et al. proposed an indoor people-counting system using a 60 GHz FMCW radar and a
spiking neural network (SNN) that processed preprocessed range–Doppler maps [23]. Its
performance was compared with that of the VGG16, ResNet-50, and MobileNet architec-
tures in scenarios involving zero to five people. Wang et al. used a Transformer network to
estimate the number of people in a tracked group from multi-frame sequences of spatial
and frequency-domain features extracted from 24 GHz MIMO FMCW radar data [24]. The
model was integrated into a tracking pipeline that enabled the simultaneous monitoring
of the group’s position and size. Zhang et al., in turn, employed an improved ResNet-50
network and fused range–time and Doppler–time spectrograms obtained using a 60 GHz
radar [25]. The system distinguished six composite classes describing the number of people
and their motion configuration and was additionally evaluated in a separate task involving
the counting of zero to three people.
The reviewed approaches address three types of tasks. The first group of methods
counts people based on trajectories crossing a predefined boundary. The second estimates
the number of people currently present in an observed scene or tracked group. The
third comprises methods that simultaneously determine the number of people passing
through the monitored area and their direction of movement from radar data [15–25].
However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, the reviewed studies do not present
a method that treats an entire passage through a doorway zone as a single event and

analyzes it using sequences of three-dimensional MIMO FMCW radar point clouds. A
solution is therefore still needed that can determine the number of entering and exiting
people without continuously tracking each individual and subsequently update the current
room occupancy.
This problem becomes particularly important when several people move in close prox-
imity, and their reflections temporarily form a single cluster or extended object. Additional
difficulties arise when people move simultaneously in opposite directions, stop within the
doorway zone, change their speed, reverse direction before crossing the threshold, or pass
by the entrance. Under such conditions, conventional tracking methods require correct
data association and trajectory continuity, whereas classification of the current number of
people in the scene does not unambiguously determine how many individuals crossed the
threshold in each direction. Furthermore, even a small number of incorrect decisions for
individual events may cause progressive drift between the estimated and actual occupancy.
Complete-event analysis reduces the dependence of the final result on the correct
separation of individuals in every frame. The model can use information available before,
during, and after the temporary merging of radar reflections and does not require persistent
person identities or uninterrupted individual trajectories. The relevant information is
contained in the evolution of the complete spatial point distribution and radial velocities
between the entrance and inner zones rather than in the continuous assignment of each
detection to a particular person.
The objective of this study is not merely to perform binary presence detection, which
can be achieved using considerably simpler sensing solutions. Instead, the objective is to
develop and evaluate a method that separately determines the numbers of entering and
exiting people for each complete doorway event and subsequently updates the current
room occupancy. Particular attention is given to challenging events in which several
people move simultaneously, including in opposite directions, and their radar reflections
temporarily merge, preventing the reliable maintenance of separate trajectories.
To achieve this objective, a hybrid event-based method was developed for bidirectional
people counting and room occupancy estimation using a single 77 GHz MIMO FMCW radar.
The unit of analysis is neither an individual frame nor the instantaneous number of people
in the observed scene, but a complete event comprising the appearance of individuals
within the doorway zone, their movement relative to the threshold, and their departure
from the monitored area.
The input data consist of sequences of three-dimensional radar point clouds together
with their corresponding radial velocities. These data are provided through the output
stream of the radar demonstration software, referred to as the out-of-box (OOB) output.
The method therefore uses data preprocessed by the radar and does not require access to
raw analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples or modification of the device firmware.
The core of the method is a multitask spatiotemporal neural network. A PointNet
encoder processes the point cloud from each frame and produces a representation of its
spatial distribution and radial velocities. A bidirectional gated recurrent unit (BiGRU)
network then models the temporal evolution of successive representations, while the
attention mechanism aggregates information from individual frames using learned weights.
This enables the model to differentiate the contribution of successive event phases to the
representation used for the final prediction. Spatial features describe the redistribution
of radar activity between the entrance and inner zones and changes in the point-cloud
geometry, whereas radial velocities provide information about the direction and dynamics
of movement. The BiGRU captures the evolution of these features throughout the complete
event. Consequently, temporary merging of reflections does not necessarily determine the
final decision when the preceding and subsequent phases contain sufficient information to

identify the event. The model independently estimates the numbers of entering (nin) and
exiting (nout) individuals, thereby enabling the analysis of events involving simultaneous
movement in both directions. The signed occupancy change for the k-th event was defined
as ∆Nk = nin,k −nout,k. An auxiliary five-class classification head identifies unidirectional
movement, simultaneous movement in both directions, reversal, lateral passage past the
entrance, and a stop followed by a return toward the doorway.
The neural network predictions were combined with geometric verification of move-
ment across the doorway plane and an assessment of decision confidence. The occupancy
state is updated only after the event has ended, the movement of radar activity between
the two sides of the threshold has been confirmed, and the adopted confidence criterion
has been satisfied. If the model output conflicts with the geometric information or its
confidence is insufficient, the event is marked as ambiguous and recorded in the system log
but does not automatically update the counter. This approach separates the interpretation
of complex events, performed by the neural model, from the deterministic mechanisms
used to verify decisions and maintain the room occupancy state.
The methodological contribution does not lie in introducing new standalone neural-
network layers, but in formulating bidirectional counting as complete-event analysis,
independently estimating entry and exit counts, and integrating spatiotemporal infer-
ence with deterministic geometric verification and occupancy-state updating. The main
contributions of this study are as follows:
1.
A formulation of bidirectional people counting as the analysis of a complete doorway-
zone event, with direct and independent estimation of the numbers of entering
and exiting individuals, rather than the classification of individual frames or the
instantaneous number of people in the scene;
2.
A multitask PointNet–BiGRU architecture with an attention mechanism that exploits
temporal changes in the geometry and radial velocities of radar point clouds, including
periods in which reflections from multiple individuals temporarily merge;
3.
The inclusion of mixed, apparent, and ambiguous events involving simultaneous
movement in both directions, reversal, lateral passage past the entrance, and stopping
without crossing the doorway threshold;
4.
The integration of neural model predictions with geometric verification of doorway
crossing and confidence assessment, together with evaluation at the individual-event
level, in terms of the long-term accumulation of occupancy-state errors, and in an
independent environment without model retraining or fine-tuning;
5.
The implementation of the complete processing pipeline using OOB data from a single
77 GHz MIMO FMCW radar, without access to raw ADC samples or modification of
the device firmware.
The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the materials
and methods, including the radar system configuration, OOB data acquisition, event
segmentation, model architecture, dataset, and evaluation metrics. Section 3 presents
experimental results, comparisons with baseline methods, and ablation studies. Section 4
discusses the results and the limitations of the proposed method, while Section 5 provides
the conclusions.
2. Materials and Methods
This section presents the radar system configuration, experimental environment, data
acquisition protocol, and the proposed method for bidirectional people counting and
room occupancy updating. It also describes the preparation and annotation of the dataset,
the model training procedure, the adopted evaluation metrics, and the computational
performance of the complete system.

2.1. Radar Hardware and OOB Data Configuration
Measurement data were acquired using a uRAD Automotive HPA v2.0 radar (Anteral
S.L., Huarte, Spain) equipped with a Texas Instruments AWR1843 device [26]. The radar
board is shown in Figure 1. This compact FMCW radar operates over a frequency range of
76–81 GHz. Its antennas are integrated into the printed circuit board, which comprises three
transmit and four receive antennas. In the configuration used in this study, all transmit
and receive channels were activated, forming a MIMO array used to estimate the three-
dimensional positions of the detected points. The field of view covers 120◦in the azimuth
plane and 40◦in the elevation plane. The radar board measures 45 × 45 × 10 mm and
weighs 5 g.
Figure 1. uRAD Automotive HPA v2.0 radar module based on the AWR1843 chipset used in the
experiments: front, rear, and side views.
The FMCW waveform configuration was prepared using mmWave Demo Visualizer
3.6.0.0 for Texas Instruments mmWave SDK 3.06. The starting frequency was set to 77 GHz,
and the chirp frequency slope was 70 MHz/µs. The chirp ramp time was 57.14 µs, while
the idle time between consecutive chirps was 267 µs. A total of 256 complex samples were
acquired during each chirp at a sampling rate of 5.209 MS/s. The total frequency sweep
bandwidth during the chirp was approximately 4.00 GHz, whereas the effective bandwidth
covered by the acquired samples was approximately 3.44 GHz. This corresponded to a
range resolution of approximately 4.4 cm.
Transmission was performed using time-division multiplexing (TDM) of the transmit
antennas. A single MIMO cycle comprised three consecutive chirps, each transmitted by a
different antenna. The cycle was repeated 16 times, resulting in 48 chirps per frame. The
frame period was 100 ms, corresponding to a frame rate of 10 frames per second. The
maximum unambiguous range was approximately 9.02 m, while the detection range in the
radar configuration was limited to 0–8.92 m. The maximum unambiguous radial velocity
was ±1.00 m/s, with a velocity resolution of approximately 0.13 m/s.
Point detection was performed using a constant false alarm rate (CFAR) algorithm,
with thresholds in the range and Doppler domains set to 15 dB. Peak grouping was
enabled in both domains, together with multi-object beamforming. Hardware-based
static clutter removal remained disabled, allowing static returns to be filtered during a
subsequent software-processing stage. The principal parameters of the radar platform and
the configuration used in this study are summarized in Table 1.

The radar was connected to the data acquisition computer through a micro-USB
interface, which provided device power, configuration transfer, and output-data reception.
The USB-to-UART bridge integrated into the radar provided two virtual serial ports. The
configuration port operated at 115,200 bit/s and was used to transmit commands from the
configuration file, whereas the data port operated at 921,600 bit/s and was used to receive
successive measurement packets.
Data were acquired using the standard out-of-the-box firmware designed for radar
point-cloud detection. The packet corresponding to each frame contained a header and type–
length–value (TLV) data blocks. For each detection, the detected-points block contained
the Cartesian coordinates together with the signed radial velocity. A supplementary side-
information block contained the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and noise level associated
with each point. The SNR and noise-level values were transmitted with a resolution of
0.1 dB. The number of points varied between frames and depended on the number of
people within the field of view, their positions, movement patterns, and the strength of the
generated reflections.
The coordinate-system origin was located at the center of the antenna array. From
the perspective of an observer positioned behind the radar, the positive X-axis pointed to
the right, the positive Y-axis pointed along the radar’s viewing direction, and the positive
Z-axis pointed upward. The velocity provided by the device was the radial velocity, i.e.,
the component of the point velocity along the line connecting the point to the radar.
2.2. Experimental Environment, Participants, and Measurement Setup
Measurements were conducted in a laboratory room measuring 5 m in width and 9 m
in length, with a floor area of 45 m2. The laboratory contained typical furnishings and
equipment, including tables, cabinets, measurement instruments, and computer hardware.

The measurement setup was located inside the laboratory, near the wall containing
the entrance and exit door. The radar was positioned near the center of the room width,
directly adjacent to the entrance zone. The sensor was mounted on a tripod at a height of
1 m above the floor and approximately 1 m from the doorway plane. The radar boresight
was directed into the laboratory, approximately along its longitudinal axis. The sensor
position and orientation remained unchanged throughout all measurement sessions.
During the measurements, the door remained fully open, and the position of its leaves
did not change. This reduced variable radar reflections caused by the opening and closing
of the door. The radar did not observe the area outside the room. Its field of view covered
the entrance zone inside the laboratory and the space extending from the doorway toward
the opposite end of the room.
The monitored area was divided into an entrance zone located directly adjacent to
the radar and doorway and an inner zone covering the more distant part of the laboratory.
When a person entered the room, radar activity first appeared in the entrance zone and
subsequently moved farther into the laboratory. During an exit, movement in the opposite
direction was observed: the activity moved from the inner zone toward the radar and
disappeared near the doorway. The event direction was therefore determined from tempo-
ral changes in the position of the radar point cloud relative to the two zones, rather than
through direct observation of both sides of the physical doorway plane. The measurement
setup comprised the uRAD Automotive HPA v2.0 radar, a tripod, a USB cable, and a
computer responsible for configuring the sensor, receiving the OOB stream, and recording
the radar point clouds. The arrangement of the principal components of the setup is shown
in Figure 2a.

A reference camera was used to record video simultaneously with radar data. The
video recordings were used exclusively to establish the ground-truth course of each event,
determine the number of people crossing the doorway threshold in each direction, and
prepare the dataset labels. The camera images were not used as input to either the proposed
method or the neural model.
Five university students aged 21–24 years participated in the experiment, including
two women and three men. All participants were informed about the purpose and proce-
dure of the experiment, the data acquisition process, and the intended use of the data in
the study. Each participant provided informed consent to participate in the measurements
and to have a reference video recorded.
The measurement protocol included both actual doorway crossings and events that
should not change the occupancy state. The first group comprised passages involving one
to five people moving in the same direction. Entry and exit events were recorded separately.
Mixed events, during which participants moved simultaneously in opposite directions,
were also investigated. All configurations involving a total of two to five participants were
included. These comprised one person entering and one exiting; two entering and one
exiting; one entering and two exiting; three entering and one exiting; two entering and two
exiting; one entering and three exiting; four entering and one exiting; three entering and
two exiting; two entering and three exiting; and one entering and four exiting.
Events that did not change the occupancy state included a participant appearing in
the entrance zone and returning toward the doorway without moving into the inner zone,
passing laterally through the entrance zone without continuing farther into the laboratory,
and stopping near the entrance before leaving the monitored area along the same path.
Actual entry and exit events involving changes in speed or brief stops were also recorded.
In such cases, after stopping, the participant continued moving between the entrance and
inner zones. This made it possible to distinguish a temporary stop during an actual entry
or exit from an event that should not update the occupancy state.
The recorded dataset comprised 550 individual events used for model development
and evaluation. Twenty repetitions were performed for each combination of people count
and movement direction. For each of the three event types that did not change occupancy
state, 50 repetitions were recorded. The dataset size represented a compromise between
scenario diversity, the ability to evaluate individual configurations, and the logistical cost
of conducting the experiment. The detailed structure of this part of the dataset is presented
in Table 2.
The measurements were conducted in five separate sessions, each comprising
110 events. In each session, four repetitions were performed for every combination of
people count and movement direction, together with ten repetitions of each event type that
did not change the occupancy state. Between successive recordings, the group composition,
participant order, spacing between individuals, and movement speed were varied.
The dataset of 550 individual events was partitioned at the level of complete measure-
ment sessions. Three sessions comprising 330 events (60%) were used for model training,
one session containing 110 events (20%) was used for validation, and the remaining ses-
sion, also comprising 110 events (20%), was reserved for the final test evaluation. Events
originating from the same session were not distributed across different dataset subsets.
In addition to the individual events, five continuous measurement sequences were
recorded, each comprising 20 consecutive events. Each sequence began from a known,
manually specified occupancy state. Between events, participants could remain stationary
within the inner zone. Their presence was still included in the reference occupancy state,
even when they did not generate stable detections in the current radar point cloud. The
sequences were therefore used to evaluate the maintenance of an occupancy state derived

2.3. Proposed Event-Based People-Counting Pipeline
The proposed method is a hybrid processing pipeline that combines event-based
analysis of radar point clouds, a multitask spatiotemporal model, and a deterministic
mechanism for maintaining the occupancy state. Following OOB data filtering and the
extraction of a complete event, the resulting sequence is processed in parallel by a geometry-
based branch and a PointNet–BiGRU model with an attention mechanism. The neural
model estimates the numbers of people moving into the room and toward the exit, assigns
the event to one of five classes, and determines the prediction confidence. The geometry-
based branch evaluates the direction and consistency of radar-activity movement between
the entrance and inner zones. The outputs of both branches are then combined, and
the occupancy state is updated only for events that satisfy the adopted confidence and
geometric-consistency criteria. The complete processing pipeline is illustrated in Figure 3.

4. Discussion, Limitations and Future Work
The results support the formulation of bidirectional people counting as the analysis
of complete events rather than the classification of individual frames or the continuous
tracking of individual trajectories. The complete method achieved accuracies of 95.5%
and 94.5% for the entry and exit counts, respectively. Both counts were simultaneously
estimated correctly for 102 of the 110 test events, corresponding to a joint entry–exit count
accuracy (JCA) of 92.7%. The mean absolute error of the signed occupancy change was 0.06
persons per event. The difference between the accuracies of the individual counting heads
and the JCA demonstrates that evaluating entry and exit counts separately may lead to an
overly optimistic interpretation of performance. Maintaining an accurate occupancy state
requires both counts to be estimated correctly within the same event.
Comparison with the baseline methods showed that geometric information alone
was insufficient to interpret complex events. The complete method increased JCA by
37.2 percentage points relative to the geometry-only rules and by 24.5 percentage points
relative to the approach based on DBSCAN clustering and tracking. At the same time, the
occupancy-state MAE decreased from 1.10 and 0.78 persons, respectively, to 0.10 person.
These results confirm that the number of radar points or temporarily identified clusters is
not a reliable proxy for the number of people, particularly when reflections from several
participants periodically merge into a single extended object.
The advantage of the event-based approach can be explained by the different infor-
mation required by the two processing strategies. A conventional tracker depends on the
continuity of separate detections and on correct frame-to-frame data association. When

reflections from people moving close to one another temporarily merge, the number of
detected clusters may decrease, existing tracks may be lost, and the subsequent separa-
tion of reflections may produce ambiguous track assignments. Simultaneous movement
in opposite directions creates an additional difficulty because detections associated with
different directions may overlap spatially near the doorway threshold. In contrast, the
proposed method does not require point-to-point correspondence, continuous individual
tracks, or persistent person identities. It uses the spatial distribution of the complete point
cloud, radial velocity, and their temporal evolution before, during, and after the period of
reduced separability.
Mechanistically, the spatial coordinates describe changes in the geometry and location
of radar activity, including its redistribution between the entrance and inner zones. Radial
velocity provides information about the direction and dynamics of movement relative to the
radar. The PointNet encoder transforms each point cloud into a frame-level representation
without assigning detections to individual people. The BiGRU integrates the evolution of
these representations across the complete event, while the attention mechanism allows the
model to assign greater importance to temporal segments associated with doorway crossing,
direction changes, temporary merging or separation of reflections, and departure from the
monitored region. Consequently, information available before and after a temporary loss
of separability can contribute to the final decision.
The highest accuracy was obtained for unidirectional movement, for which the JCA
reached 97.5%. For simultaneous movement in opposite directions, this value decreased to
85.0%. Mixed events therefore remain the most challenging scenario because the model
must independently recover two counts from partially overlapping reflections. The de-
terioration in performance with increasing group size had a similar cause. The JCA was
100% for events involving one or two people but decreased to 83.3% for five people. This
indicates that the primary limitation is not recognition of the general direction of movement
but separation of the contributions of individual people under mutual occlusion and with
a limited number of radar-generated points.
The five-class event-type head achieved an accuracy of 97.3%, demonstrating the
ability to distinguish actual passages and mixed events from behaviors that did not change
the occupancy state. This is particularly important for reversals, lateral passages, and stops
followed by a return toward the doorway because their initial segments may resemble an
actual entry or exit. Auxiliary event-type classification reduced the risk of interpreting
short-term activity near the doorway as a completed threshold crossing. This was confirmed
by the ablation study, in which removing the auxiliary head reduced JCA from 92.7% to
88.2% and increased the long-term occupancy-state error.
The largest deterioration in the ablation study occurred after removing the BiGRU
network. The JCA decreased to 80.0%, while the occupancy-state MAE increased from 0.10
to 0.42 person. This indicates that a single-frame representation does not contain sufficient
information to reliably recognize the complete course of an event. Radial velocity and the
attention mechanism were also important. Removing radial velocity reduced JCA to 88.2%,
whereas removing the attention mechanism reduced it to 89.1%. Radial velocity supple-
mented geometric information with movement dynamics, while the attention mechanism
allowed greater importance to be assigned to sequence segments associated with doorway
crossing, direction changes, or departure from the monitored area.
The interpretability analysis presented in this study remains limited to a mechanistic
interpretation of the input features and network components supported by the ablation
results. Intermediate representations, event-specific attention weights, and frame-level
model responses were not archived during the original experiments. Consequently, these
quantities could not be reliably reconstructed for the events included in the reported evalu-

ation without retraining the model and obtaining a different model realization. Rather than
presenting newly generated visualizations as results of the original experiment, the revised
manuscript provides a more detailed explanation of how spatial features, radial velocity,
and temporal changes contribute to the final decisions. Future work should include the sys-
tematic recording and visualization of intermediate representations, attention distributions,
and key-frame responses for representative mixed events and cases involving temporary
merging of reflections.
Geometric-consistency verification and the confidence criterion had the greatest effect
on long-term occupancy-state accuracy. Removing them did not change the raw JCA of the
neural-network outputs but increased the occupancy-state MAE to 0.22 and 0.27 person,
respectively. This demonstrates that individual-event classification accuracy does not fully
describe the utility of a counting system. Even a small number of incorrect decisions may
accumulate over successive updates; therefore, the ability to reject an ambiguous event is
an important component of the method. The most favorable trade-off was obtained using a
confidence threshold of 0.80, for which coverage reached 94.5%, selective accuracy reached
98.1%, and the occupancy-state MAE was 0.10 person. Further increasing the threshold
improved the accuracy of accepted decisions but rejected too many actual passages, causing
the counter error to increase again.
Evaluation using five continuous sequences confirmed that the method could maintain
the occupancy state without continuously detecting the people present in the room. Across
100 consecutive events, the occupancy-state MAE was 0.10 person, and the mean absolute
final error was 0.20 person per sequence. This result is relevant to applications such as
heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning control, which require information about current
occupancy rather than the continuous localization of every occupant. However, the method
maintains the occupancy state on the basis of accepted entry and exit events and does not
directly detect stationary people already present in the room.
The cross-environment experiment provided additional evidence regarding the trans-
ferability of the proposed method. When the model trained exclusively using data from
the original laboratory was applied to 100 events recorded in the second laboratory, the
joint entry–exit count accuracy decreased from 92.7% to 91.0%. Entry-count, exit-count,
and event-type accuracies reached 94.0%, 92.0%, and 96.0%, respectively, while the mean
absolute error of the signed occupancy change increased only from 0.06 to 0.07 person per
event. These results were obtained without retraining, fine-tuning, parameter adaptation,
or modification of the decision thresholds. The limited performance reduction suggests
that the model captured spatiotemporal characteristics of complete doorway events that
were not restricted to the geometry of the original laboratory. Nevertheless, because the
evaluation involved only one additional environment, this result should be regarded as
preliminary evidence of cross-environment generalization.
Direct comparison of the obtained values with the results reported in studies [15–25]
requires caution. The cited methods use different radar frequencies, signal representations,
class definitions, numbers of participants, measurement geometries, and data-partitioning
procedures. Some evaluate trajectory-tracking accuracy, whereas others evaluate scene-
count classification or movement-direction recognition. In contrast, the results presented in
this study concern the simultaneous estimation of entry and exit counts within a complete
event and the resulting occupancy-state updates. The performance gains should therefore
be assessed primarily relative to the baseline methods evaluated using the same test dataset.
The first limitation concerns the number and diversity of the measurement environ-
ments. Although the model was additionally evaluated in an independent laboratory
without retraining or parameter adaptation, the study included only two rooms and two
doorway configurations. The cross-environment experiment therefore provides preliminary

evidence of generalization rather than comprehensive validation across different buildings
and operating conditions. Further experiments are required to determine the robustness of
the method to wider variations in room geometry, doorway width, equipment arrangement,
radar distance, mounting height, mounting angle, and measurement-region configuration.
The second limitation is the dataset size. The model was developed using 330 training
events, and the primary evaluation was conducted using a single held-out test session
comprising 110 events. This partitioning enabled an independent session-level evaluation,
but the results for less frequent configurations, particularly groups of four and five people,
are subject to greater uncertainty. The independent laboratory dataset contained an addi-
tional 100 events, but these measurements were intended specifically for cross-environment
evaluation and did not increase the diversity of the training data. Future studies should
increase the number of sessions, participants, and repetitions and should evaluate several
independent session-based splits or apply leave-one-session-out validation. Reporting
confidence intervals for the principal metrics would also be appropriate.
The dataset comprised five predefined event categories and did not cover all behaviors
that may occur at a real doorway. The study did not consider, among other cases, people
carrying large objects, strollers or carts, children and adults with substantially different
body sizes, prolonged presence within the doorway zone, or consecutive groups whose
radar activity did not disappear between passages. In such cases, the event-segmentation
mechanism may combine several passages into a single long sequence. Extending the
dataset with events outside the known class set should be accompanied by a method for
detecting out-of-distribution cases.
The adopted maximum sequence length and number of points also constitute limi-
tations. Events were represented using no more than 80 frames and 64 points per frame.
Farthest point sampling preserves the spatial extent of the point cloud but may remove
weaker reflections associated with some participants. Similarly, uniform sampling of events
lasting longer than 8 s may reduce the visibility of brief motion phases relevant to recogniz-
ing a doorway crossing. Future work should evaluate the effects of temporal resolution and
point count and consider models capable of processing variable-length sequences without
reducing them to a fixed size.
The use of a bidirectional GRU network means that a decision can be made only after
an event has ended. This is consistent with the adopted counter-update procedure but
prevents the final occupancy change from being determined while a passage is still in
progress. Moreover, inference time, memory consumption, and model operation on a target
embedded platform were not evaluated separately. Before the system can be used to control
building equipment, its total latency must be determined, including event-start and event-
end detection, tensor preparation, model inference, geometric-consistency verification, and
occupancy-state updating.
The method uses point clouds generated by the radar’s OOB software. This facilitates
implementation and eliminates the need to process raw ADC samples, but it also makes
the input quality dependent on the detector configuration and the algorithms implemented
in the device. Reflections from partially occluded individuals may be discarded before the
data are passed to the model. Generalization to other radar devices or configurations will
therefore require verification of data-format compatibility, detection characteristics, and the
distribution of point counts.
The long-term evaluation comprised a total of 100 events, which made it possible to
observe error accumulation and compensation but did not represent multi-day system
operation. Because the counter is updated recursively, a single missed entry or exit may
maintain a discrepancy between the ground-truth and estimated occupancy states over
many subsequent events. Rejecting events protects the system from updates based on

ment may therefore require a mechanism for periodic correction or reinitialization of the

Future work should include measurements in additional rooms with more diverse
doorway widths and radar mounting configurations, larger numbers of participants and
scenarios, evaluation of cross-subject generalization, and longer continuous sequences.
It will also be important to investigate causal models that make decisions using only
the observed portion of an event, adaptive confidence criteria, methods for detecting
out-of-distribution events, and procedures for automatically correcting the occupancy
state. Systematic recording and visualization of intermediate representations, attention
distributions, and key-frame responses should also be included to provide a more direct
interpretation of model decisions. These studies will help determine the extent to which the
proposed method can be transferred from controlled laboratory environments to long-term
operation in real buildings.
5. Conclusions
This study developed an event-based method for bidirectional people counting and
room occupancy estimation using OOB point clouds generated by a single 77 GHz MIMO
FMCW radar. Rather than continuously tracking individual people, the proposed approach
treats a complete doorway passage as a single event. The PointNet encoder represents the
spatial distribution of radar points in individual frames, the BiGRU models the temporal
evolution of these representations before, during, and after temporary merging of reflec-
tions, and the attention mechanism assigns greater importance to the most informative
phases of the event. Separate output heads estimate the numbers of entering and exiting
people, while geometric-consistency verification and the confidence criterion reduce the
risk of incorrect occupancy-state updates.
In the original held-out test session, the complete method achieved a joint entry–exit
count accuracy of 92.7% and a mean absolute error of 0.06 persons per event for the signed
occupancy change. Across five continuous sequences comprising 100 events, the mean
occupancy-state MAE was 0.10 person. The comparative and ablation studies confirmed
the importance of temporal modeling and demonstrated the advantage of the proposed
hybrid method over geometry-only rules and an approach based on DBSCAN clustering
and tracking.
In the independent laboratory, the model achieved a joint entry–exit count accuracy
of 91.0% and a mean absolute error of 0.07 persons per event without retraining, fine-
tuning, or parameter adaptation. This limited performance reduction provides preliminary
evidence that the learned event representation can be transferred between different mea-
surement environments. Nevertheless, further evaluation involving additional rooms,
doorway geometries, radar mounting configurations, participants, and longer continu-
ous measurements is required before the method can be considered suitable for general
real-world deployment.
